title: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary · Units 50–51 (editorially reviewed)
description: Units 50–51 reviewed against the teaching pages, examples, illustrations, exercises and answer key. The content covers conjunctions, contrasting functions, comparison words, addition, calendar vocabulary, day/month abbreviations, seasons and time prepositions. Original English examples, Brazilian Portuguese translations and British English IPA.
sourceNotice: The supplied textbook was checked for learning targets, distinctions and exercise coverage. Example sentences and explanatory notes are original; textbook activities and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Unit 50: teaching sections A–B, conjunction and comparison tables, exercises 50.1–50.5 and answer key. Unit 51: teaching sections A–C, timeline and seasonal illustrations, exercises 51.1–51.6 and answer key. Reviewed each target, translation, example, British IPA and source provenance.
audit.pronunciation: British English, largely non-rhotic IPA. Checked the source transcriptions for month, hour, Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and autumn; compound-phrase pronunciations are editorial transcriptions with possible natural connected-speech variants.
audit.cannotGuarantee: The actual VocabLab 1.2 Lite importer, browser speech synthesis, pronunciation scoring, adaptive review, and backup/restore have not been tested. Phrase IPA is not individually confirmed against an external pronunciation dictionary.

editorialReview.reviewMethod: Direct review of PDF text and rendered teaching/exercise pages, comparison with the answer key, item-by-item English-language and IPA review, stable-ID and JSON structural checks.
editorialReview.notes: English is used in all fields except the pt translations. Source-reviewed means a learning target is grounded in the source, not that an original example sentence is quoted. Entries marked pedagogical-extension expand on the taught pattern.

units.title: Unit 50 — Conjunctions and connecting words
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd ed., Unit 50, textbook pp. 106–107 (PDF pp. 107–108); original example sentences.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.pt: conjunção; palavra que liga partes de uma frase
items.example: “Because” is a conjunction in this sentence.
items.note: A conjunction connects words, phrases or clauses. It can show addition, contrast, choice, reason, result, time or condition.

items.pt: conectivo; palavra que estabelece uma relação entre ideias
items.example: Use a connecting word to join these two ideas.
items.note: A general term for words that connect ideas; this unit also includes adverbs and comparison words.

items.example: I have a sister and two brothers.
items.note: And joins additional information or actions. It does not by itself indicate a reason or contrast.

items.pt: e fomos para casa (ligação entre orações)
items.example: The museum closed, and we went home.
items.note: And can join two clauses, e.g. We finished and we went home. This particular phrase is an original teaching extension of the conjunction pattern.

items.example: I like coffee, but my sister prefers tea.
items.note: But introduces contrast between two ideas; unlike and, it signals a difference or unexpected result.

items.example: Would you prefer water or juice?
items.note: Or introduces alternatives, choices or other possibilities. It may connect words or clauses.

items.example: We stayed inside because it was very cold.
items.note: Because introduces the reason: result + because + reason. Contrast so, which introduces a result.

items.example: The shop was closed, so we went home.
items.note: So introduces a consequence: reason or situation + so + result. Do not swap because and so without adjusting the sentence.

items.example: Call me when you arrive at the station.
items.note: When introduces the time of an event. In future time clauses, present simple is normally used after when.

items.example: Wash your hands before you make lunch.
items.note: Before means that an event takes place earlier than another: A before B means A happens first.

items.example: We had coffee after we finished the lesson.
items.note: After means that an event takes place later than another: A after B means B happens first.

items.example: If it rains, we will stay at home.
items.note: If introduces a condition that may or may not be satisfied. It contrasts with when for an expected time or event.

items.example: I will visit you if I have time tomorrow.
items.note: A common future conditional pattern is if + present simple, with will in the main clause. The source exercises practise if with future reference.

items.example: Because it was late, we took a taxi, so we got home quickly.
items.note: Because gives a reason; so gives a result. The two words express different directions of the causal link.

items.example: When you arrive, call me; if your train is late, send me a message.
items.note: When usually locates an event in time; if makes the event conditional. These words can both refer to the future.

items.example: Before we leave, please check the windows; after we arrive, we can have lunch.
items.note: Before puts the event in the main clause first; after puts the event in the subordinate clause first.

items.example: I have only ten minutes before my class.
items.note: Only restricts an amount, duration, number or frequency. Its position may change what is restricted.

items.example: I have visited that museum only once.
items.note: Only once means on one occasion and no more. This complete phrase is an additional example of only with a frequency expression.

items.example: Your new coat looks like mine.
items.note: Here like makes a comparison, rather than expressing enjoyment. In look like, it introduces the person or thing being compared.

items.example: The two sisters look like their mother.
items.note: Look like + noun or pronoun means resemble. Compare the verb like, which can express preference.

items.example: My uncle swims like a fish.
items.note: Like + noun can compare the way someone does something with an animal or object. Exercise 50.3 practises this comparison.

items.example: A train is usually longer than a car.
items.note: Than follows comparative adjectives or adverbs, e.g. better than or harder than. Do not confuse than with then.

items.example: She plays the piano better than I do.
items.note: Better is an irregular comparative of good and well. Than introduces the second part of a comparison.

items.pt: mais intensamente do que; mais difícil do que
items.example: My brother studies harder than I do.
items.note: Harder is the comparative of hard; it can refer to greater effort or greater difficulty, depending on context.

items.example: My cousin lives in Bristol, and my aunt also lives there.
items.note: Also usually comes before the main verb or after be. It adds information, like too and as well.

items.example: I like this film, and my friends like it too.
items.note: Too commonly comes at the end of a clause when it means also; too can also mean excessively in other contexts.

items.example: She wants to learn German as well.
items.note: As well often occurs at the end of a clause to add information; it is different from as well as.

items.example: Our neighbour works at the hospital, and his wife works as well.
items.note: Also, too and as well express addition. Compare She also works, She works too, and She works as well.

learningObjectives: Join information using and, contrast ideas with but, and introduce alternatives with or.
Distinguish the reason introduced by because from the consequence introduced by so.
Use when, before, after and if to express time relationships, sequence and conditions.
Use only for restricted amounts or frequency, like for similarity and than in comparisons.
Add related information with also, too and as well, recognising their usual positions.
Choose appropriate linking words in context and produce original sentences using the patterns from sections A and B.

units.title: Unit 51 — Days, months, seasons
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd ed., Unit 51, textbook pp. 108–109 (PDF pp. 109–110); original example sentences.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.example: There are twenty-four hours in a day.
items.note: A day has 24 hours. Use a capital letter for the names of particular days of the week.

items.example: There are seven days in a week.
items.note: A week has seven days. The days of the week are written with initial capital letters.

items.example: We are going on holiday for a fortnight.
items.note: A fortnight means two weeks (14 days). It is particularly common in British English.

items.example: There are twelve months in a year.
items.note: A year has 12 months. The plural is months /mʌnθs/; compare the spelling and sound of Monday.

items.example: Three months is a long time to wait.
items.note: Months is the plural of month; notice the consonant sequence /nθs/ at the end.

items.example: My course starts next year.
items.note: An ordinary year has 365 days; a leap year has 366 days.

items.example: There are 366 days in a leap year.
items.note: A leap year has 366 days, including 29 days in February. Exercise 51.2 reinforces this distinction.

items.example: The journey takes an hour.
items.note: The letter h is silent, so use an hour, not a hour. One hour is 60 minutes.

items.example: Wait a minute, please.
items.note: A minute contains 60 seconds. In this meaning minute is pronounced /ˈmɪnɪt/.

items.example: The light was green for only a few seconds.
items.note: One minute has 60 seconds. Second can also be an ordinal number in another context.

items.example: This building is more than a century old.
items.note: A century is a period of 100 years.

items.pt: um quarto de hora; quinze minutos
items.example: The meeting starts in a quarter of an hour.
items.note: A quarter of an hour is 15 minutes. This exact question appears in exercise 51.6.

items.example: Sunday is my favourite day of the week.
items.note: Sun is a common abbreviation. English day names always begin with a capital letter.

items.example: I have an English class on Monday.
items.note: Mon is a common abbreviation. Use on Monday, not in Monday.

items.example: We visit the library on Tuesday.
items.note: Tue and Tues are common abbreviations. The day name is capitalised.

items.example: The meeting is on Wednesday.
items.note: Wed is a common abbreviation. The first d in the spelling is not separately pronounced.

items.example: My birthday is on Thursday this year.
items.note: Thu and Thurs are common abbreviations. The initial th represents the voiceless /θ/ sound.

items.example: Our lessons finish on Friday.
items.note: Fri is a common abbreviation. The name of a day begins with a capital letter.

items.example: The shop opens early on Saturday.
items.note: Sat is a common abbreviation. Saturday and Sunday together make up the weekend.

items.example: We often visit our family at the weekend.
items.note: The weekend normally means Saturday and Sunday. British English commonly uses at the weekend.

items.example: I went to the cinema at the weekend.
items.note: Use at the weekend in the British English pattern taught here, not in the weekend. On the weekend is common in American English.

items.example: My new course begins on Monday.
items.note: Use on with a named day: on Monday, on Friday, on Saturday.

items.example: I have a dance class on Tuesday evening.
items.note: Use on before a particular day and part of the day: on Tuesday evening, not in Tuesday evening.

items.example: I finished the book yesterday.
items.note: Yesterday means the day before today. It can answer a question beginning When ...?

items.example: Today is Wednesday, so I have a lesson.
items.note: Today means the present day; compare yesterday and tomorrow on the diagram in section B.

items.example: We are going to the market tomorrow.
items.note: Tomorrow means the day after today.

items.example: I saw my cousin the day before yesterday.
items.note: The day before yesterday means two days before today; the timeline and exercise 51.6 reinforce it.

items.example: Our friends are arriving the day after tomorrow.
items.note: The day after tomorrow means two days after today; the timeline and exercise 51.6 reinforce it.

items.example: I drink tea every morning.
items.note: The textbook uses morning for the hours before 12 noon. A specific day takes on: on Monday morning.

items.example: She works at home in the afternoon.
items.note: The textbook describes afternoon as the period from 12 noon to 6 pm. Use on Monday afternoon for a specific day.

items.example: We usually eat together in the evening.
items.note: The textbook describes evening as the period after 6 pm. Use on Tuesday evening for a specific day.

items.example: The doctor called me on Monday morning.
items.note: Capitalise Monday. When giving a specific time of the week, use on Monday morning.

items.example: The class finishes on Monday afternoon.
items.note: For a particular day and part of the day, say on Monday afternoon.

items.example: We practise English on Monday evening.
items.note: For a particular day and part of the day, say on Monday evening.

items.example: Classes begin in January.
items.note: Jan is the common abbreviation. January has 31 days; use in January when naming only the month.

items.example: Her birthday is in February.
items.note: Feb is the common abbreviation. February has 28 days, or 29 in a leap year.

items.example: We moved here in March.
items.note: Mar is the common abbreviation. March has 31 days and begins with a capital letter.

items.example: The festival is in April.
items.note: Apr is the common abbreviation. April has 30 days and begins with a capital letter.

items.example: My sister finishes university in May.
items.note: May is normally written in full. As a month name, it begins with a capital letter and has 31 days.

items.example: We usually have a holiday in June.
items.note: June is normally written in full. It has 30 days; use in June, not on June, without a specific date.

items.example: The weather is warm in July.
items.note: July has 31 days and has stress on the second syllable: /dʒuˈlaɪ/.

items.example: My parents are travelling in August.
items.note: Aug is the common abbreviation. August has 31 days and starts with a capital letter.

items.example: The course starts in September.
items.note: Sep and Sept are common abbreviations. September has 30 days.

items.example: Our school opens in October.
items.note: Oct is the common abbreviation. October has 31 days.

items.example: We visited them in November.
items.note: Nov is the common abbreviation. November has 30 days.

items.example: There are many celebrations in December.
items.note: Dec is the common abbreviation. December has 31 days.

items.example: We spend more time outdoors in spring.
items.note: Season names normally begin with lowercase letters. Both in spring and in the spring are natural.

items.example: They go to the beach in summer.
items.note: Season names normally use lowercase letters. Both in summer and in the summer are possible.

items.example: The leaves change colour in autumn.
items.note: Autumn is common in British English; fall is also used, especially in American English. The final written n in autumn is silent.

items.example: We wear warm coats in winter.
items.note: Season names normally use lowercase letters: in winter or in the winter.

items.example: There are four seasons in this country.
items.note: The four seasons named here are spring, summer, autumn and winter; normally they are not capitalised.

items.example: My birthday is in July.
items.note: Use in with the month alone: in July, not on July. Use on with a specific date: on 15 July.

items.example: The gardens look lovely in the spring.
items.note: Both in spring and in the spring are correct; this pattern also works with other seasons.

items.example: We will meet on Friday.
items.note: Use on with a particular day: on Friday, on Wednesday evening. Use in with a month or season.

items.example: We sometimes travel in December.
items.note: Use in with a month or season, e.g. in December and in winter, not on December.

items.pt: escrever o dia da semana e a data
items.example: Write the day and date in your notebook before class.
items.note: The textbook recommends writing the weekday and date in English to practise calendar vocabulary and capitals.

items.pt: quinze minutos; um quarto de hora
items.example: A quarter of an hour is enough for a short break.
items.note: Quarter of an hour is a natural part of longer expressions such as a quarter of an hour. The source quiz tests the meaning: 15 minutes.

learningObjectives: Name units of time from seconds to centuries and recognise the time equivalences taught in the book.
Recognise, spell and capitalise the seven days of the week, including their common abbreviations.
Use today, yesterday, tomorrow, the day before yesterday and the day after tomorrow to locate events in time.
Use morning, afternoon, evening and the weekend; distinguish on + weekday from at the weekend.
Recognise and capitalise the twelve months and their abbreviations, including month lengths and leap years.
Name spring, summer, autumn and winter with their usual lowercase spelling; use in with months and seasons and practise writing dates.
